flagged.evidence: Step 2.1 says that when a block lies in K one can “rewrite it as the canonical element of K and push it across.” Decidable membership supplies only a yes/no test. The cited normal-form theorem supplies normal forms relative to fixed transversals, chosen non-effectively, and does not provide an algorithm translating a discovered element of K in G to its corresponding word in H. Such effective embedding/translation data is necessary for the advertised algorithm.

The cited normal-closure result explicitly says that for n=0 the displayed product is the identity. For P=<x | emptyset> and the empty word w, w is null and has area 0, but there is no positive-length relator expression because R is empty. Thus the assertion that the defining set contains “at least one positive integer m” is false.

The stated class includes the finite presentation P=<x | emptyset>, but step 1.1 defines M=max{|r|:r in R}. Here R is empty, so this maximum is undefined. No empty-relator-set case is separated before M is used to define the search bound.

Steps 1.1–2.1 show only that one semidecision procedure may fail to halt on negative inputs. That does not show that no different decision algorithm exists: a recursive language can also have a halting-only semidecider. A refutation needs an unsolvable-word-problem recursive presentation, such as the Novikov-Boone example; none is invoked here.

Take the triangle graph with all groups trivial, T={a,b}, and T'={b,c}. In pi_1(G,T), c is the sole non-tree generator. The prescribed map sends c to p_T'(o)c p_T'(t)^(-1), but all T' path terms and c are trivial in pi_1(G,T'), since c is a T' edge. Hence c maps to 1, so the claimed composites cannot fix every non-tree generator as step 3.1 asserts.

The proof removes a non-tree edge e. Since the chosen maximal subtree T remains after deleting e, the original graph stays connected; after collapsing T, e is a loop at the sole collapsed vertex and likewise cannot disconnect. Thus the claimed amalgam alternative never supplies the missing tree-of-groups induction, yet steps 2.1–3.1 use it to conclude the result for arbitrary graphs.

[L1] states only that reduced words of positive edge length are nonidentity. A nonidentity element of G_v has edge length 0, so [L1] does not license the claim that it remains nonidentity in the ambient group. The required zero-edge-length uniqueness or vertex-group-injectivity clause is neither stated nor proved.

The definition independently chooses a lift for every oriented quotient edge, but does not require the reverse choices to satisfy tilde(bar e)=bar(tilde e). It then sets G_e=Stab(tilde e). The graph-of-groups definition requires G_e=G_(bar e) for a geometric edge; independently chosen reverse lifts generally have conjugate, not equal, stabilizers. Therefore the prescribed data need not form a graph of groups.

Step 3.1 calls Psi G-equivariant and surjective because every point of T lies in the G-orbit of a chosen lift. Its image, however, is only the Phi(pi_1(G,T_0))-orbit until surjectivity of Phi is proved; no G-action on the source is defined without already identifying G with the source. Step 4.1 then uses the asserted isomorphism Psi to conclude that Phi is an isomorphism, making the argument circular.

The example permits arbitrary m,n but calls k->mk and k->nk “two monomorphisms.” If m=0 or n=0, the corresponding map Z->Z is not injective, contrary to the graph-of-groups definition requiring injective boundary maps. The graph-of-groups realization therefore needs m,n nonzero.
